lines.text: Why this matters
M11 taught how analytical files and table metadata are arranged. M12 answers the next question: what
happens when one process is no longer enough to scan, join and aggregate the data comfortably? Spark
separates coordination from parallel task execution. The point is not 'big data magic'; it is a concrete
execution model you can reason about when work is divided across partitions.
Picture it in your head
Picture a restaurant pass. The driver is the head coordinator reading the order tickets and deciding the
plan. Executors are kitchens that do assigned work. A partition is a tray of records given to one task at a
time. A task is one unit of work over one partition for one stage. In local[2] the whole restaurant is still
your laptop: two local task threads can work concurrently, but you have not created two production
worker machines.
New words before we use them
driver = application coordinator; executor = process that runs tasks and stores data for an application;
partition = chunk of distributed data; task = unit of work for one partition in one stage; cluster manager =
service that allocates resources in a real cluster; local[2] = local master with two worker threads.

Follow with me once
Run the pure-Python architecture simulator first so the terms are stable before Spark is installed. Then, on
the learner PC, run `01_architecture_partitions.py`. Record `defaultParallelism`, the input partition count
and row count. The 18-row dataset is intentionally tiny: we are learning the execution model, not proving
Spark is faster than Python on 18 rows.
python practice/simulators/distributed_reasoning_simulator.py --section architecture
# learner PC with PySpark:
cd practice/spark
python 01_architecture_partitions.py
What you should see
The simulator says the driver plans/co-ordinates, executors run tasks over partitions, and local[2] is two
local task threads. The Spark lab should report 18 source rows. Partition counts can differ by reader and
environment; the lesson is to inspect them rather than memorise a number.
Why it worked
Spark can parallelize because the logical dataset is split into partitions and tasks can operate on
independent partitions. The driver does not personally process every row just because Python started the
application. Keeping this distinction prevents later errors such as bringing all data back to the driver with
collect().
Break it / common failure
Do not say 'a partition is a server' or 'one row equals one task.' One executor can process many partitions
over time, and one partition can contain many rows. Also do not infer a production cluster from local[2].
Local mode is a useful execution engine on one machine, not distributed hardware.
Reason through a realistic incident
A learner sees four tasks in the Spark UI and says there must be four executors. Diagnose the claim. Ask
which stage ran, how many partitions it had, what master was used, and where executor processes
actually live. Task count follows partition work; it is not an executor count.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
The useful abstraction is layered: your DataFrame code describes a computation, the driver
builds/optimizes a plan, stage boundaries appear where dependencies require data exchange, and tasks
execute stage work per partition. Resource allocation and task scheduling are related but not the same
thing. This layered model lets you debug from the outside in: first business result, then DataFrame plan,
then stage/task evidence, then resource symptoms.
Now you do a changed version alone
Draw driver -> stage -> tasks -> partitions from memory. Explain what changes and what does not
change when the same 18-row job moves from local[2] to a real cluster. Name two things that can scale
out and two business-correctness rules that must remain identical.
Fresh changed retry
A stage has 80 partitions and the cluster has 8 executor cores available. Explain why 80 tasks do not run
simultaneously and why reducing to 8 partitions automatically is not always the right repair.

Inspect the smallest independent control first: source row/key totals, pure-Python validator or

Then inspect Spark structure: schema, partitions, explain plan, and on the learner PC the UI/runtime

Ready-made revision
Use the execution model to explain evidence, not as vocabulary theatre. For every Spark incident be able
to state where the code runs, which operation created the partition boundary, what one output row
means and which row/key/total check proves business correctness.
Evidence / mastery
Save code, actual result/error, one independent row/key/amount control, relevant plan/runtime evidence,
a 60-90 second explain-back and the changed retry. If Spark itself was not executed, label the runtime
part PENDING rather than converting static/simulator evidence into a fake runtime PASS.
Why this matters
A Spark lesson is useless if setup advice encourages an 8 GB laptop to run like a production cluster. The
goal is a small, reproducible local lane that exercises the same DataFrame APIs while keeping resource
use bounded. Current PySpark 4.2.0 supports Python 3.10+ and requires Java 17+; the course profile
uses local[2], 1g driver memory and four shuffle partitions so plans stay visible on a modest machine.
Picture it in your head
Think of a flight simulator rather than an airport. The controls and rules are real, but the scale is
intentionally small. SparkSession is your cockpit entry point. local[2] tells Spark to use two local worker
threads. The four-shuffle-partition setting makes tiny examples readable; it is not a recommendation that
production jobs should always have four partitions.
New words before we use them
SparkSession = structured API entry point; master = execution location such as local[2] or a cluster
manager; driver memory = heap available to the driver JVM; shuffle partitions = default number of
partitions for many SQL shuffle outputs; AQE = runtime adaptive optimization; JAVA_HOME =
environment pointer to Java installation.

On the learner PC, create a clean virtual environment and pin `pyspark==4.2.0`. Run `java -version`,
`python --version` and `00_env_probe.py`. Then create the session using `common.py`, print the four
settings and stop the session. This review release does not certify live PySpark execution. The learner PC
must prove the SparkSession starts and the commands run with the stated settings.
python -m venv .venv
# activate .venv, then:
pip install -r practice/spark/requirements.txt
java -version
python practice/spark/00_env_probe.py
What you should see
Your learner environment should report PySpark 4.2.0, a supported Python version and Java 17 or later. A
SparkSession created through `common.spark_session()` should use local[2], 1g driver memory,
`spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=4` and AQE true. Record the actual values rather than assuming
configuration took effect.
Why it worked
A pinned small environment separates course logic from machine noise. When every lab uses the same
session builder, a plan difference is less likely to be caused by one forgotten setting. Explicitly stopping
sessions also reduces the chance that multiple JVMs compete for your limited RAM.
Break it / common failure
Common setup mistakes are mixing system Python and venv Python, installing multiple Spark versions,
assuming Java 8/11 guidance from an old video is current, or opening Airflow/Docker/PostgreSQL/Spark
together on an 8 GB laptop. Another mistake is treating `pip install pyspark` success as proof that a Spark
job actually starts.
Reason through a realistic incident
`import pyspark` works, but SparkSession fails with a Java gateway error. Do not rewrite the pipeline.
Check `java -version`, `JAVA_HOME`, the active Python environment and PySpark version first. A runtime
bootstrap failure happens before your transformation logic is evaluated.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Version pinning is part of reproducibility, not administrative overhead. Spark spans Python, Py4J and a
JVM runtime; failures can originate at multiple layers. Record versions with the same evidence as code.
Later modules can choose a different pinned environment when another library has stricter compatibility;
do not force one global environment merely for convenience.

Why this matters
Spark DataFrames are not giant Python lists. They are distributed, schema-bearing logical datasets whose
operations can be inspected and optimized. Explicit schemas matter because engineering pipelines
should not repeatedly guess whether `qty` is text or integer, whether a field is nullable, or whether a
malformed value should silently change the inferred type.
Picture it in your head
Picture a warehouse receiving form. Before boxes arrive, the form says order_id is text, order_date is a
date, qty is integer and unit_price is decimal-like numeric. A DataFrame carries that contract with the
rows. Spark can reason about named typed columns; a Python loop over arbitrary dictionaries hides much
of that structure from the optimizer.
New words before we use them
DataFrame = distributed table-like dataset with named columns; schema = column
names/types/nullability; StructType/StructField = explicit schema objects; Column expression = symbolic
computation evaluated by Spark; inference = reader guesses types from data; Catalyst = optimizer
framework behind Spark SQL/DataFrames.

Open `common.py` and inspect `ORDER_SCHEMA`. Then run `02_dataframe_schema.py`. It reads
`orders.csv` with the explicit schema, derives `gross_sales = qty * unit_price`, selects four columns and
shows them in deterministic order for inspection. Compare this with reading the same CSV without a
schema and ask what assumptions Spark would have to make.
cd practice/spark
python 02_dataframe_schema.py
# inspect common.py before the run
What you should see
The schema should show typed date/integer/double fields instead of all strings. The resulting DataFrame
keeps one row per source order and adds `gross_sales` without collecting the whole dataset into Python.
The source fixture remains 18 rows.
Why it worked
Built-in column expressions remain part of Spark's structured plan. Explicit types let Spark validate
operations and choose encodings without first treating everything as Python objects. More importantly,
the data contract becomes reviewable: another engineer can see what the pipeline expects before a bad
batch reaches a downstream join.
Break it / common failure
Do not assume explicit schema means bad values are automatically quarantined with useful reasons;
input error behavior still needs a contract. Do not mark every field nullable just to avoid errors. And do not
confuse schema with grain: a perfect schema cannot tell you whether one row is one order, item or event
unless you state it.
Reason through a realistic incident
A new file contains `qty='five'`. With loose inference, behavior may vary depending on the reader/data
sample. With an explicit integer contract, the mismatch becomes visible at the ingestion boundary.
Decide whether the source row should fail, become null under an explicit policy, or be quarantined
upstream; do not silently reinterpret the business field.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Schema is one of three correctness layers in this module: schema says what columns mean and how
values are typed; grain says what one row represents; keys/cardinality say how rows may combine. Many
Spark bugs happen because engineers validate only one layer. Keep all three in evidence notes,
especially before joins and aggregations.

Why this matters
Spark SQL and the DataFrame API are two ways to describe many of the same structured computations.
You should be able to translate between them because teams mix notebooks, SQL models and Python
jobs. The important skill is semantic equivalence: same input population, same output grain, same
grouping/filter rules and independently matching totals.
Picture it in your head
Picture two languages giving instructions to the same query planner. One says `df.filter(...).groupBy(...)`;
the other says `SELECT ... WHERE ... GROUP BY ...`. If both describe the same logic, the engine can
optimize them through the same structured subsystem. Syntax familiarity is secondary to proving that
the two requests really mean the same thing.
New words before we use them
temporary view = session-scoped name exposing a DataFrame to SQL; expression equivalence =
different syntax produces the same intended result; semantic equivalence = same business meaning, not
merely similar-looking code; SQL plan = optimizer representation of SQL/DataFrame operations.

Follow with me once
Run `03_sql_equivalence.py`. The DataFrame route filters Completed orders, groups by region and sums
gross sales. The SQL route queries a temporary view with the same rule. Sort both by region before
comparison. Expected totals are East 5950, North 6380, South 6000 and West 6900.
cd practice/spark
python 03_sql_equivalence.py
What you should see
Both routes produce four regional rows with identical totals; their sum is 25,230. The result grain is one
row per region. If one route includes Pending/Cancelled rows or uses a different calculation, matching
syntax style is irrelevant because business semantics differ.
Why it worked
DataFrame and SQL expressions enter Spark's structured optimizer. Translating between them makes
assumptions visible: WHERE/filter defines the population, groupBy/GROUP BY changes the grain, and
aggregate expressions define measures. Sorting is added only to make evidence comparisons
deterministic, not because DataFrames are inherently ordered.
Break it / common failure
A common false comparison is `df.show()` versus a SQL query with `ORDER BY` and assuming row-order
difference means value mismatch. DataFrames are not guaranteed ordered unless you request ordering.
Another mistake is registering a view before adding `gross_sales`, then writing SQL that assumes the
column already exists.
Reason through a realistic incident
The Python job reports West 6900 while an analyst's SQL reports West 7800. Before blaming Spark,
compare filters, gross-sales formula, null handling and source version. Use a shared temporary view or
small fixed fixture to isolate semantic differences.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Equivalence is useful for debugging because SQL can make group/filter logic obvious while DataFrame
code makes programmatic composition obvious. But duplicated logic can drift. In production, choose a
clear ownership boundary rather than maintaining two hand-copied implementations forever; use
equivalence tests during migration or review.

Why this matters
Spark DataFrame transformations are lazy: constructing a filter/select/groupBy chain usually builds a plan
rather than immediately scanning the full source. An action such as count, show, collect, write or first
asks Spark to execute enough of that plan to produce a result. This matters because repeated actions can
repeat work unless persistence or prior output changes the execution path.
Picture it in your head
Imagine writing a recipe on a whiteboard. Adding 'filter Completed' and 'group by region' changes the
recipe, but the kitchen does not cook yet. `show()` is the order bell. Spark now turns the recipe into an
executable plan and schedules jobs. A second bell can cause another execution if results were not
persisted or materialized elsewhere.
New words before we use them
transformation = returns a new logical dataset; action = requests a result or side effect that triggers
execution; lazy evaluation = defer execution until needed; lineage = dependency chain used to derive
data; action boundary = point where computation must produce something observable.

Follow with me once
Run `04_lazy_plans.py`. The script creates a filter -> withColumn -> groupBy chain, prints a message
before any action, calls `explain('formatted')`, then uses `show()`. Notice that explain inspects the plan
while show requests output. Later, use the Spark UI on your learner PC to associate actions with jobs

cd practice/spark
python 04_lazy_plans.py
What you should see
Before `show()`, you have a DataFrame plan object, not four already-calculated regional totals sitting in
Python memory. The action produces the four totals. The exact number of jobs/stages can depend on
Spark/version/operation; inspect runtime evidence rather than promising one fixed count from the source
code alone.
Why it worked
Laziness gives Spark room to optimize a whole structured plan: it can push filters, prune columns or
change join strategy rather than executing each line as an isolated Python instruction. The cost is
conceptual: source code order is not a timeline of physical execution.
Break it / common failure
Do not say 'nothing happens' before an action in an absolute sense: analysis/planning and metadata work
can occur, and some operations may interact with catalog/source metadata. The important boundary is
that full data computation is deferred. Also do not call `count()` casually after every debugging line; each
action can trigger real work.
Reason through a realistic incident
A notebook has five `display/count/show` calls between transformations and runs much slower than a
single final write. Explain that the notebook may be triggering multiple executions. Remove unnecessary
actions, use plan inspection/bounded checks, or cache only if repeated reuse justifies it.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Action discipline is a reliability skill as much as a performance skill. An action can write output, move data
to the driver or materialize cache. Before running it, know whether it is read-only, driver-bound, or
side-effecting. Later orchestration should treat output-writing actions as explicit boundaries with
idempotency rules.

Why this matters
When an action triggers Spark, the driver turns the optimized plan into executable work. Jobs are created
by actions; jobs are split into stages around shuffle/exchange boundaries; stages contain tasks,
commonly one per partition. `DataFrame.explain()` is your first window into the plan, while the Spark UI
on a real runtime shows what actually executed.
Picture it in your head
Picture a road trip with toll bridges. Long stretches of local road can be completed without everyone
regrouping. A shuffle boundary is like a bridge where records with the same destination key must be
redistributed before the next stretch can start. Each stretch becomes a stage; each lane/partition gets a
task.
New words before we use them
job = computation triggered by an action; stage = group of tasks that can run without a shuffle
dependency between them; Exchange = physical-plan node often indicating redistribution; physical plan
= chosen execution operators; Spark UI = runtime evidence for jobs/stages/tasks/storage/SQL; explain =
textual plan inspection.

What you should see
The plan should show a distributed aggregation path with an Exchange/shuffle boundary for grouping by
region. Runtime stage/task counts depend on partitions and adaptive execution; do not hard-code a
universal number into your explanation.
Why it worked
Rows with the same group key can begin in different input partitions. To compute a final per-region sum,
Spark must bring compatible key groups together. That cross-partition dependency creates a stage
boundary. The physical plan gives a hypothesis; runtime statistics tell you how the actual execution
behaved.
Break it / common failure
Do not label every operation a shuffle. Simple select/filter/withColumn can often remain narrow.
Conversely, do not assume a groupBy is cheap because the result has only four rows; many source rows
may have moved before those four results appeared. Small output is not small work.
Reason through a realistic incident
A job outputs four rows but takes minutes at scale. The analyst says 'only four rows, Spark is slow.'
Explain how a four-row aggregation can require scanning billions of rows and shuffling keys. Inspect scan,
Exchange and task metrics instead of reasoning from output size.
Deepen the engineering reasoning
Plans have logical, optimized and physical layers. You do not need to memorise every node. Learn to
locate scans, filters, projections, exchanges, joins and aggregates; then ask whether each is expected
from the business request. Performance tuning begins only after correctness and expected plan shape
are understood.

Why this matters
Partition count controls how work and data are divided, but changing it is not a universal speed knob.
`repartition()` can increase or decrease partitions and typically redistributes data; `coalesce()` is
commonly used to reduce partitions with a narrower dependency when possible. Both can be useful, and
both can be harmful when used without file-size/workload evidence.
Picture it in your head
Imagine four boxes of books. Repartition is like emptying books onto a sorting table and rebuilding boxes
according to a new rule or count. Coalesce is like combining neighboring boxes into fewer boxes without a
full resort when Spark can do so. The final box count may match, but the work taken to get there can
differ.
New words before we use them
repartition = reshuffle into a requested partitioning; coalesce = reduce partitions with limited movement
where possible; narrow dependency = child partition depends on a small set of parent partitions;
parallelism = tasks that can potentially execute concurrently; output-file count = often related to partition
count at write time, not identical in every sink.

Why this matters
The Spark driver is not a free dumping ground. `collect()` returns all rows to the driver process;
`toPandas()` similarly materializes the DataFrame as a pandas object on the driver. Both can be
appropriate for deliberately small bounded results, but calling them on unknown-large data can crash the
application even when executors have plenty of memory.
Picture it in your head
Picture a distributed warehouse with many shelves but one office desk. Spark can store/process boxes
across shelves, yet `collect()` tells every shelf to send its selected contents to that one desk. If you know
the result is five rows, fine. If you request a billion rows, the desk is the bottleneck.

limit = logical bound before retrieval; distributed write = keep output distributed instead of returning to
driver.
